Accessing Peekbank Data

2026-10-20

Source: vignettes/peekbankr.Rmd
peekbankr.Rmd

Overview

The peekbankr package allows you to access data in the peekbank database from R. Data are hosted in the versioned peekbank dataset on Redivis; the client retrieves tidy tables from it without you having to write queries. This vignette shows some examples of how to use the data loading functions and what the resulting data look like.

Every table in the release is a field on the client, holding the whole table:

  • pb$datasets
  • pb$subjects
  • pb$administrations
  • pb$trials
  • pb$trial_types
  • pb$stimuli
  • pb$aoi_region_sets
  • pb$aoi_timepoints
  • pb$xy_timepoints

To work with part of a release, pb$subset$<table>() takes dplyr expressions. For the timepoint tables, which are far too large to narrow locally, these run on the server.

Technical note 1: The first request will open a browser window to authorize Redivis access (or set a REDIVIS_API_TOKEN).

Technical note 2: Start by creating a client with peekbank(). It pins a database version for your whole analysis, and every table you read from it comes from that same version. The version is required, because Peekbank is re-released over time and an unpinned script quietly reads different data as those releases land. Pass "current" if you do want whichever version is newest, which is not always the highest release number. The older connect_to_peekbank() / get_*(connection = con) style still works.

Technical note 3: We have tried to optimize the time it takes to get data from the database (the AOI timepoints transfer run-length-encoded and are expanded locally). But if you query entire timepoint tables, it will still take a while, as you are transferring 100s of MB of data.

# load the library
library(peekbankr)

# pin a database version for all the calls below
pb <- peekbank("2026.1")

Get datasets

The datasets field holds a table related to the sources of the dataset, information of the tracker, information of the method (e.g., monitor size and sample rate).

For example, reading pb$datasets gives you every dataset in the database.

d_datasets <- pb$datasets
head(d_datasets)

Get Subjects

The subjects field holds information about persistent subject identifiers for noting when subjects have participated in multiple experiments. This includes demographic information (currently only sex and lab-specific subject id).

d_subjects <- pb$subjects
head(d_subjects)

Auxiliary data

Several tables carry a *_aux_data column holding whatever a lab recorded that the schema has no place for. It arrives as a JSON string, so it is not much use until you unpack it. unpack_aux_data() turns every *_aux_data column in a table into a nested column of the fields it holds:

d_subjects_aux <- unpack_aux_data(pb$subjects)
names(d_subjects_aux$subject_aux_data[[1]])
#> "lang_exposures" "cdi_responses" "lang_measures" "native_language_non_iso"

From there tidyr::unnest() twice gets you to rows; once to lift the fields out of the nested column, once to expand whichever field you want:

cdi <- unpack_aux_data(pb$subjects) %>%
  tidyr::unnest(subject_aux_data) %>%
  filter(!is.na(cdi_responses)) %>%
  tidyr::unnest(cdi_responses)

Predicates can reach the column before it is unpacked, but only as text, since the server sees a JSON string:

pb$subset$aoi_timepoints(grepl("cdi_responses", subject_aux_data))

Get Administrations

The administrations field holds information about the specific experimental administrations to subjects in the database. This includes information about:

  • age
  • monitor size
  • tracker

Again, if you run the function with no arguments, then you get all the information for all administrations in the database, but you can now also filter on a dataset name or dataset id.

d_administrations <- pb$subset$administrations(dataset_name == "pomper_saffran_2016")
head(d_administrations)

The age argument takes a number indicating the age(s) of children (in months) that you want to analyze. you can use this argument in two ways

  1. Pass a single number to get information about all participants who were tested at that particular age.
  2. Pass a range of ages to get information about all participants who were tested within a certain age range.

For example, you can get the participant information for all of the children who were tested between the ages of 24 and 36 months.

d_age_range <- pb$subset$administrations(age >= 24, age <= 36)
head(d_age_range)

Get trials

The trials field holds a table with information of the trials in the experiments in the database. This includes the following information:

  • Phrase
  • Language
  • Point of disambiguation
  • IDs to link to other tables.
d_trials <- pb$trials
head(d_trials)

This function also takes dataset name and id filters.

Get stimuli

The stimuli field holds a table with information of the stimuli in the experiments in the database. This includes the following information:

  • Label
  • Image
  • Novelty status
d_stimuli <- pb$stimuli
head(d_stimuli)

This function also takes dataset name and id filters.

Get AOI region sets

The aoi_region_sets field holds a table with the information of the region of area of interest (AOI) for experiments using eye-trackers. It includes information of the dimensions of the x and y, such as the minimum and maximum dimension of the xy spaces.

d_aoi_region_sets <- pb$aoi_region_sets
head(d_aoi_region_sets)

This function is not expected to be used commonly - this information is retained as part of the process of calculating AOIs from XY points.

Get AOI timepoints

The aoi_timepoints field holds a table with information of the subject’s looking behavior in each trial. For example, you can get information about which area that the subject was looking at in a particular trial (e.g., looking away or target or distractor).

Narrow it with pb$subset$aoi_timepoints(), which takes dplyr expressions that run on the server. As everywhere in pb$subset, an expression can name any column of the table or of anything a row of it belongs to. A timepoint belongs to an administration — with its dataset and subject (dataset_name == "pomper_saffran_2016", age < 24, sex == "female") — and to a trial, with its trial type and its two stimuli (vanilla_trial, !excluded, target_stimulus_novelty == "familiar"). These are expressions rather than named arguments, so == and not =.

The t_norm field provides a trial-normalized time variable (milliseconds) whose 0 point is the point of disambiguation on that trial (first timestep of the onset of the first time the target label is said).

d_aoi_timepoints <- pb$subset$aoi_timepoints(dataset_name == "pomper_saffran_2016")
head(d_aoi_timepoints)

Get XY timepoints

For experiments using eye-trackers (as opposed to hand coding from video), the xy_timepoints field holds a table including the x and y position across time.

d_xy_timepoints <- pb$subset$xy_timepoints(dataset_name == "reflook_v4")

Query without downloading

pb$db holds a dbplyr handle on each table. dplyr verbs on these compile to SQL and run on the server, and nothing is transferred until you collect(). The handles carry the same columns as the fields above, so a summary over a timepoint table costs you four rows rather than 36 million.

pb$db$aoi_timepoints %>%
  count(aoi) %>%
  collect()

pb$db also holds aoi_timepoints_rle, the run-length encoded form the aoi_timepoints field expands locally: one row per run of a constant AOI, with length the number of 25 ms samples in the run.
